idiom_name: SQLAlchemy relationship(secondary=...) over an association table
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy's canonical form is a Core Table holding the two foreign keys (both primary_key=True) passed as relationship(secondary=association_table): the ORM then inserts, deletes and joins link rows itself, and the collection attribute behaves like any other relationship. This is Association Table Mapping at its most direct - the table exists in the metadata, but no mapped class represents it. Keep it while the link has no payload; use selectinload or lazy='selectin' so a collection load is one batched query per page instead of one per object.
code_sketch:
association_table = Table(
    "actor_film", Base.metadata,
    Column("actor_id", ForeignKey("actor.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True),
    Column("film_id", ForeignKey("film.id", ondelete="CASCADE"), primary_key=True))

class Actor(Base):
    __tablename__ = "actor"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    films: Mapped[list["Film"]] = relationship(
        secondary=association_table, lazy="selectin", back_populates="actors")
pitfalls: Relying on database ON DELETE CASCADE without passive_deletes=True makes SQLAlchemy load/delete association rows itself, adding queries; configure passive_deletes when the database, not the ORM, should clean the link table.
Configuring passive_deletes=True without matching ON DELETE CASCADE leaves orphan link rows when a parent is deleted -> add the database cascade or keep ORM cleanup enabled.

Deleting an element from the collection issues DELETE for its link row, but assigning a fresh list re-reads the existing rows - with lazy loading that is a per-item query unless the collection is loaded.
secondary targets the table by name or object; pointing two relationships at the same table without back_populates produces two independent writers of the same link rows.
The association table needs a real key on the pair: without primary_key/unique on both columns SQLAlchemy creates plain columns and duplicate links get inserted freely.
ORM-level cascade does not replace database-level ON DELETE CASCADE: deleting a parent without loading the collection (or without passive_deletes) leaves orphan rows.

variants.name: SQLAlchemy association object mapped as a class
variants.implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy documents the association object as the upgrade path: the link table becomes a mapped class with the two foreign keys as its key columns plus any payload, and the ends relate to it with one-to-many relationships. The association is then a first-class object that can be created, inspected and extended, at the price of longer navigation (actor.actor_films[0].film instead of actor.films). This is the association-entity promotion of the pattern, and the right form as soon as the association carries data.
variants.code_sketch:
class ActorFilm(Base):
    __tablename__ = "actor_film"
    actor_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("actor.id"), primary_key=True)
    film_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("film.id"), primary_key=True)
    cast_since: Mapped[date | None]
    actor: Mapped["Actor"] = relationship(back_populates="actor_films")
    film: Mapped["Film"] = relationship(back_populates="actor_films")

class Actor(Base):
    __tablename__ = "actor"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    actor_films: Mapped[list[ActorFilm]] = relationship(back_populates="actor")

class Film(Base):
    __tablename__ = "film"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    actor_films: Mapped[list[ActorFilm]] = relationship(back_populates="film")
pitfalls: Navigation gets longer and every caller must now create the link object explicitly - a real cost, not an implementation detail.
delete-orphan on the association collection is what removes link rows when a link is dropped; a plain one-to-many leaves the row behind.
The composite key is immutable: changing one side of a link is a delete plus an insert.
variants.idiom_name: SQLAlchemy association object mapped as a class

variants.name: Django ManyToManyField with an explicit through model
variants.implementation_notes: In Django the relation is declared on the models: ManyToManyField creates the join table implicitly (and the admin and ORM manage the links for you), and passing through=SomeModel hands the join table to a model you define, which is required as soon as the association needs extra fields. The implicit form is a two-line declaration; the through form is the association-entity promotion with the same accessors plus direct access to the link rows. Choose it when Django owns the persistence layer; the mapper work the pattern describes is inside the framework.
pitfalls: With an explicit through model the manager's add()/set() helpers only work while the through model has no extra required fields; once the association needs a required payload column, link rows are created as ordinary model instances instead.
The implicit join table already enforces uniqueness of the pair (Django's auto-created through model declares it) but cannot carry data; adding a payload later means a migration to the through form.

on_delete on the through model's foreign keys decides orphan behaviour - CASCADE removes the links with the object, PROTECT refuses to delete it while links exist - so both must be chosen deliberately.
variants.idiom_name: Django ManyToManyField with an explicit through model
